es.summary: Pérdida de sangre del tracto gastrointestinal que puede originarse en cualquier segmento y presentarse como vómito con sangre o heces negras o rojas.
key_points: La hemorragia puede ser alta (esófago, estómago) o baja (intestino, colon, recto).
Signos de sangrado oculto incluyen anemia y disminución de la presión arterial.
Endoscopia es la prueba diagnóstica de elección para localizar y tratar la causa.
El manejo inicial incluye reposición de volumen y, si es necesario, transfusión.
Complicaciones graves: shock hipovolémico, insuficiencia renal y sepsis.

pathophysiology: Daño a la mucosa o lesión vascular produce ruptura de vasos y pérdida de sangre.
La sangre se mezcla con contenido gastrointestinal, alterando la absorción de nutrientes y electrolitos.
La pérdida continua disminuye el volumen intravascular, provocando hipoperfusión tisular.
risk_factors: Úlceras pépticas y uso crónico de AINES.
Enfermedad inflamatoria intestinal (colitis ulcerosa, enfermedad de Crohn).
Diverticulosis, varices esofágicas y tumores gastrointestinales.
signs_symptoms: Vómito con sangre roja brillante o con aspecto de posos de café.
Heces negras (melena) o con sangre roja brillante (hematochezia).
Dolor abdominal y sensación de desmayo.
diagnostics: Hemograma: hemoglobina <10 g/dL indica pérdida significativa.
Pruebas de coagulación (TP, TTP) para descartar coagulopatías.
Endoscopia digestiva alta o colonoscopia según sospecha de origen.
Radiografía de abdomen o TC en casos de sangrado masivo no endoscopiable.
treatment: Reposición de volumen con cristaloides (solución salina al 0.9%).
Transfusión de concentrado de glóbulos rojos si Hb <7 g/dL o síntomas de hipoxia.
Inhibidores de bomba de protones (omeprazol) por vía IV para úlceras pépticas.
Octreótido para sangrado de varices esofágicas.
Terapia endoscópica (coagulación, ligadura) o cirugía si el sangrado persiste.
complications: Anemia severa con fatiga y disnea.
Sepsis si hay perforación o infección secundaria.
nursing_care: Monitorear signos vitales cada 15‑30 min; observar hipotensión y taquicardia.
Evaluar nivel de conciencia y perfusión periférica (capilaridad, piel húmeda).
Mantener acceso IV de calibre amplio; registrar ingesta y salida de líquidos.
Observar y registrar características de vómito y heces (color, cantidad).
Preparar al paciente para endoscopia: ayuno y posición decúbito lateral izquierdo si hay hematemesis.
patient_teaching: Informar sobre signos de alarma: vómito con sangre, heces negras, mareos.
Evitar AINES y alcohol; seguir dieta blanda y rica en fibra según indicación.
Importancia de asistir a controles endoscópicos y de tomar medicación prescrita.
En caso de recaída, acudir inmediatamente al servicio de urgencias.

interventions.action: Administrar solución salina al 0.9% por vía IV según orden médica.
interventions.rationale: Restablece el volumen intravascular y previene el shock.

interventions.action: Monitorear signos vitales y presión arterial cada 15 minutos.
interventions.rationale: Detecta rápidamente deterioro hemodinámico.

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de conciencia y perfusión periférica (tiempo de relleno capilar).
interventions.rationale: Indicadores tempranos de hipoperfusión tisular.

interventions.action: Registrar ingesta y salida de líquidos, incluyendo drenajes y vómitos.
interventions.rationale: Permite balance hídrico preciso.

interventions.action: Preparar al paciente para transfusión de sangre si la Hb es <7 g/dL o hay síntomas de hipoxia.
interventions.rationale: Mejora la capacidad de transporte de oxígeno.

related_to: uso de diuréticos si se administran
outcomes: Sin arritmias relacionadas a alteraciones electrolíticas

interventions.action: Obtener y registrar electrolitos séricos al ingreso y cada 6‑8 horas.
interventions.rationale: Detecta desequilibrios tempranos.

interventions.action: Administrar soluciones electrolíticas (por ejemplo, Ringer lactato) según prescripción.
interventions.rationale: Corrige déficit de sodio y potasio durante la reposición de volumen.

interventions.action: Monitorear ritmo cardíaco mediante ECG continuo.
interventions.rationale: Identifica arritmias inducidas por hipopotasemia o hipernatremia.

interventions.action: Evaluar signos de alteración electrolítica: debilidad muscular, parestesias, confusión.
interventions.rationale: Permite intervención oportuna antes de complicaciones graves.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de informar vómitos persistentes o diarrea que puedan agravar la pérdida de electrolitos.
interventions.rationale: Facilita la detección precoz de nuevos desequilibrios.

en.summary: Loss of blood from the gastrointestinal tract that can originate in any segment and present as vomiting with blood or black or red stools.
key_points: Hemorrhage can be high (esophagus, stomach) or low (intestine, colon, rectum).
Signs of occult bleeding include anemia and decreased blood pressure.
Endoscopy is the diagnostic test of choice to locate and treat the cause.
Initial management includes volume replacement and, if necessary, transfusion.
Severe complications: hypovolemic shock, renal failure, and sepsis.

pathophysiology: Damage to the mucosa or vascular lesion causes vessel rupture and blood loss.
Blood mixes with gastrointestinal contents, altering nutrient and electrolyte absorption.
Continuous loss decreases intravascular volume, causing tissue hypoperfusion.
risk_factors: Peptic ulcers and chronic NSAID use.
Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease).
Diverticulosis, esophageal varices, and gastrointestinal tumors.
signs_symptoms: Vomiting with bright red blood or coffee‑ground appearance.
Black stools (melena) or bright red blood (hematochezia).
diagnostics: CBC: hemoglobin <10 g/dL indicates significant loss.
Coagulation tests (PT, aPTT) to rule out coagulopathies.
Upper GI endoscopy or colonoscopy depending on suspected source.
Abdominal X‑ray or CT in cases of massive bleeding not amenable to endoscopy.
treatment: Volume replacement with crystalloids (0.9% saline solution).
Red blood cell concentrate transfusion if Hb <7 g/dL or hypoxia symptoms.
IV proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) for peptic ulcers.
Endoscopic therapy (coagulation, ligation) or surgery if bleeding persists.
complications: Severe anemia with fatigue and dyspnea.
Sepsis if perforation or secondary infection occurs.
nursing_care: Monitor vital signs every 15‑30 minutes; watch for hypotension and tachycardia.
Assess level of consciousness and peripheral perfusion (capillary refill, moist skin).
Maintain large‑caliber IV access; record fluid intake and output.
Observe and document characteristics of vomitus and stools (color, amount).
Prepare patient for endoscopy: fasting and left lateral decubitus position if hematemesis.
patient_teaching: Inform about warning signs: vomiting with blood, black stools, dizziness.
Avoid NSAIDs and alcohol; follow a soft, high‑fiber diet as directed.
Importance of attending endoscopic follow‑ups and taking prescribed medication.
If symptoms recur, seek emergency care immediately.

interventions.action: Administer 0.9% saline solution IV as ordered.
interventions.rationale: Restores intravascular volume and prevents shock.

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs and blood pressure every 15 minutes.
interventions.rationale: Detects rapid hemodynamic deterioration.

interventions.action: Assess level of consciousness and peripheral perfusion (capillary refill time).
interventions.rationale: Early indicators of tissue hypoperfusion.

interventions.action: Record fluid intake and output, including drains and vomitus.
interventions.rationale: Allows precise fluid balance.

interventions.action: Prepare patient for blood transfusion if Hb <7 g/dL or hypoxia symptoms.
interventions.rationale: Improves oxygen transport capacity.

outcomes: No arrhythmias related to electrolyte disturbances

interventions.action: Obtain and record serum electrolytes on admission and every 6‑8 hours.
interventions.rationale: Detects early imbalances.

interventions.action: Administer electrolyte solutions (e.g., Ringer's lactate) as prescribed.
interventions.rationale: Corrects sodium and potassium deficits during volume replacement.

interventions.action: Monitor cardiac rhythm with continuous ECG.
interventions.rationale: Identifies arrhythmias induced by hypokalemia or hypernatremia.

interventions.action: Assess signs of electrolyte disturbance: muscle weakness, paresthesias, confusion.
interventions.rationale: Allows timely intervention before serious complications.

interventions.action: Educate patient on the importance of reporting persistent vomiting or diarrhea that could worsen electrolyte loss.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates early detection of new imbalances.

summary.0.quote: Signs of bleeding in the upper digestive tract include: Bright red blood in vomit Vomit that looks like coffee grounds Black or tarry stool Dark blood mixed with stool Signs of bleeding in the lower digestive tract include: Black or tarry stool Dark blood mixed with stool Stool mixed or coated with bright red blood

key_points.0.quote: Your digestive or gastrointestinal (GI) tract includes the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine or colon, rectum, and anus.

key_points.2.quote: The test used most often to look for the cause of GI bleeding is called endoscopy .

key_points.3.quote: Patients with GI bleeding may require IV fluid replacement or multiple blood transfusions to restore lost blood volume (DiGregorio & Alvey, 2022).

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: There are many possible causes of GI bleeding, including hemorrhoids , peptic ulcers , tears or inflammation in the esophagus, diverticulosis and diverticulitis , ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease , colonic polyps , or cancer in the colon , stomach or esophagus .

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Signs of bleeding in the upper digestive tract include: Bright red blood in vomit Vomit that looks like coffee grounds Black or tarry stool Dark blood mixed with stool

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: Common assessment findings for patients with acute GI bleeding are: abdominal pain or cramping anemia cool, clammy skin decreased LOC decreased urine output hematemesis (bloody vomitus) hypoactive bowel sounds hypotension melena (bloody stools) and/or dark tarry stools tachycardia

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: Pale skin, tachycardia, and hypotension may indicate significant blood loss.

sections.treatment.2.quote: Most patients experiencing bleeding from stress ulcers will also be recommended to take a PPI such as omeprazole (e.g., Prilosec) or pantoprazole (Protonix) to decrease gastric acid secretion and allow for complete healing of the ulcer.

sections.treatment.3.quote: If the bleeding originates from esophageal varices, octreotide (Sandostatin) can be used to stop the bleeding.
